stem:
A 28-year-old man with a 6-year history of treatment-resistant schizophrenia is due his week 12 clozapine review after commencing the medication at your community mental health team. He has tolerated titration to 300 mg nightly with a good clinical response, no sedation limiting function, and no cardiac symptoms. His weekly full blood count over the first 12 weeks has consistently shown a neutrophil count between 3.2 and 4.4 x10 to the 9 per litre (2.0-7.5).

He attends monitoring reliably and lives with his mother who supports his adherence. He has no history of febrile illness in the past week, no oral ulceration on examination, and no fever today. His electrocardiogram at week 6 was normal with a QTc of 400 milliseconds. Fasting lipids, glucose and weight are being tracked separately at the metabolic clinic.

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: haemoglobin 148 g/L (130-180), white cell count 6.8 x10 to the 9 per litre (4.0-11.0), neutrophil count 4.2 x10 to the 9 per litre (2.0-7.5), platelets 240 x10 to the 9 per litre (150-400)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate frequency of full blood count monitoring from now on, assuming the neutrophil count remains in the green range?

options.text: Continue weekly full blood count monitoring indefinitely irrespective of the total duration of clozapine treatment or stable results
options.rationale: Lifelong weekly monitoring is not required. AU protocols reduce frequency after the first 18 weeks and again after 12 months in the green range. (Source: Clopine Central Australian Clozapine Monitoring Protocol)
source_refs: Clopine Central Australian Clozapine Monitoring Protocol

options.text: Extend the interval immediately to monthly full blood counts because his neutrophil count has been consistently in the safe range now
options.rationale: Monthly monitoring is only after 12 months of stable therapy under Clopine. At week 12 this is too infrequent and misses the peak risk period. (Source: Clopine Central Australian Clozapine Monitoring Protocol)
source_refs: Clopine Central Australian Clozapine Monitoring Protocol

options.text: Discontinue routine haematological monitoring on the basis of a very reassuring 12-week neutrophil trend and repeat only if unwell
options.rationale: Discontinuing routine haematological monitoring is unsafe. Agranulocytosis can occur at any point during clozapine therapy. (Source: Clopine Central Australian Clozapine Monitoring Protocol)
source_refs: Clopine Central Australian Clozapine Monitoring Protocol

options.text: Switch to weekly white cell differential counts only (omit full blood count) to reduce phlebotomy burden on the patient significantly
options.rationale: The full blood count including neutrophil count is required (not white cell count alone) and this remains part of the AU protocol. (Source: Clopine Central Australian Clozapine Monitoring Protocol)
source_refs: Clopine Central Australian Clozapine Monitoring Protocol

options.text: Reduce the monitoring interval from weekly to fortnightly full blood counts and continue at that interval until the end of month 12
options.rationale: Under both AU Clopine and Clozaril monitoring programs the interval is weekly for the first 18 weeks in Clozaril and monthly after week 18. The Clopine schedule reduces from weekly to fortnightly (2-weekly) after week 18 and moves to monthly at 12 months. At week 12 he remains on weekly monitoring under either protocol; however most AU services now use the harmonised Clopine schedule and a fortnightly interval is the correct next step at week 18. The best available answer here reflects that transition when he reaches the second monitoring phase.
source_refs: Clopine Central Australian Clozapine Monitoring Protocol

explanation.summary: The AU harmonised clozapine monitoring interval is weekly for the first 18 weeks, then fortnightly (2-weekly) to 12 months, then monthly thereafter if the neutrophil count remains in the green range. The step-down from weekly to fortnightly at week 18 is the correct next transition for this patient.
key_points: Weekly FBC for first 18 weeks; fortnightly to month 12; monthly thereafter if green range
Amber and red ranges have their own AU actions (increased monitoring, cease and refer)
Metabolic monitoring runs in parallel and is not a substitute for haematological monitoring
explanation.pearls: The switch from weekly to fortnightly is the first major schedule change. Do not stop weekly early even if the neutrophil count is reassuring.

stem:
A 30-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder is commenced on lithium carbonate 250 mg twice daily by the community mental health team after a manic relapse successfully managed with olanzapine as inpatient. Her baseline pretreatment bloods showed a thyroid stimulating hormone of 2.2 mU/L (0.4-4.0), creatinine of 62 micromol/L (45-90) with eGFR greater than 90 mL/min/1.73 m2, calcium of 2.32 mmol/L (2.10-2.55), and a normal electrocardiogram.

She has no significant medical comorbidity and is not on any nephrotoxic medication. She has been counselled on adequate hydration, avoidance of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and the early symptoms of lithium toxicity (tremor, nausea, confusion). She has effective contraception in place with a levonorgestrel intrauterine system.

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: sodium 140 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), creatinine 62 micromol/L (45-90), calcium 2.32 mmol/L (2.10-2.55), TSH 2.2 mU/L (0.4-4.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate schedule of serum lithium level checks after starting therapy?

options.text: Check a random serum lithium level after 24 hours of therapy to detect early toxicity and adjust the dose against target range
options.rationale: A random 24-hour level does not reflect steady state and cannot be interpreted against therapeutic ranges. Steady state is reached at 5 to 7 days. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Mood Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Mood Disorders

options.text: Check the first level 5 to 7 days after starting or after any dose change, drawn 12 hours post-dose, then weekly until stable and 3-monthly thereafter
options.rationale: Trough (12-hour) lithium levels are checked 5 to 7 days after commencement (or dose change) to allow steady state, then weekly until stable in the target range, then 3-monthly for maintenance. AMH and RANZCP support this cadence. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Mood Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Mood Disorders

options.text: Do not check any serum lithium levels routinely; monitor clinically for tremor and confusion and only check if symptoms emerge
options.rationale: Serum lithium level monitoring is mandatory given the narrow therapeutic index (0.6 to 1.0 mmol/L acute, 0.4 to 0.8 mmol/L maintenance) and cannot be replaced by clinical monitoring alone. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Mood Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Mood Disorders

options.text: Check the first lithium level at 8 hours post-dose to capture the peak concentration and avoid missing early lithium toxicity signs
options.rationale: Trough levels 12 hours post-dose are standard. Peak levels are not the reference range and would overestimate therapeutic status. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Mood Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Mood Disorders

options.text: Check monthly lithium levels only after 4 weeks of therapy irrespective of any dose adjustments made in that starting period
options.rationale: Monthly levels delay adjustment during titration. Levels are needed 5 to 7 days after each dose change until stable. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Mood Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Mood Disorders

explanation.summary: Lithium levels are drawn as trough (12-hour post-dose) samples 5 to 7 days after commencement or any dose change, then weekly until stable in the target range, then 3-monthly for maintenance. Renal function, TSH, and calcium are monitored 6-monthly on maintenance, or more frequently if abnormal.
key_points: Trough 12-hour post-dose sample only; peak or random levels cannot be interpreted
Target 0.6 to 1.0 mmol/L for acute mania; 0.4 to 0.8 mmol/L for maintenance
6-monthly renal function, TSH and corrected calcium on maintenance
explanation.pearls: The commonest lithium level error is a random or peak sample. Book the blood draw so it is 12 hours after the previous evening dose.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Mood Disorders

stem:
A 29-year-old primigravid woman is reviewed at 34 weeks gestation. She has been taking sertraline 100 mg daily for major depressive disorder for the past 3 years, achieved remission before conception, and continued sertraline throughout pregnancy after a shared decision-making discussion at booking. She has remained euthymic during this pregnancy with Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale scores between 4 and 7 at each antenatal appointment. She has no anxiety symptoms and no suicidal ideation.

A colleague at another practice has suggested tapering sertraline over the next fortnight to reduce the risk of neonatal adaptation syndrome. She feels well and would prefer to continue her current dose. She has no personal history of postnatal depression and no family history of perinatal mental illness. She has strong social supports and a partner who has attended perinatal mental health education sessions with her.

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits
data_table.Screening tools: EPDS score 6 today, no self-harm ideation, no anxiety symptoms endorsed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate recommendation about her sertraline for the remainder of the pregnancy?

options.text: Taper sertraline over 2 weeks to zero and switch to psychological therapy alone for the remainder of the pregnancy to avoid neonatal effects
options.rationale: Tapering in the third trimester in a euthymic woman risks maternal relapse. Neonatal adaptation is self-limiting; maternal relapse is not. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Practice Guideline

options.text: Reduce the sertraline dose to 50 mg daily for the remainder of pregnancy to minimise neonatal adaptation while preserving benefit
options.rationale: There is no evidence that a lower dose reduces neonatal adaptation and it introduces risk of maternal relapse. Continue the effective dose. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Practice Guideline

options.text: Continue sertraline 100 mg daily at the current dose and inform the neonatal team so they can monitor for transient neonatal adaptation
options.rationale: RANZCP perinatal guidance is to continue effective SSRI therapy in the third trimester when the woman is euthymic and stable, because the risk of maternal relapse (with its own effects on mother, fetus and infant) exceeds the risk of self-limited neonatal adaptation syndrome. The paediatric team is informed to monitor the baby for 24 to 48 hours. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Practice Guideline

options.text: Switch to fluoxetine 20 mg daily on the basis of the longest track record of use in third-trimester pregnancy studies to date
options.rationale: Switching a stable, tolerated antidepressant risks destabilisation. Sertraline is a preferred SSRI in perinatal use and there is no advantage in changing. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Practice Guideline

options.text: Add an intramuscular corticosteroid course now to reduce the risk of neonatal adaptation syndrome after birth by promoting neonatal maturation
options.rationale: Antenatal corticosteroids are for lung maturation in threatened preterm birth, not to prevent neonatal adaptation from SSRI exposure. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Practice Guideline

explanation.summary: A euthymic woman on an effective SSRI in the third trimester should continue treatment. Discontinuation risks maternal relapse (with worse outcomes than neonatal adaptation), and dose reduction does not reliably reduce neonatal effects. The paediatric team is informed so the baby can be observed for 24 to 48 hours for transient jitteriness, feeding difficulty, or respiratory distress.
key_points: Sertraline is a preferred perinatal SSRI due to low breastmilk transfer
Neonatal adaptation syndrome is transient and self-limited; usually resolves within 2 weeks
Maternal relapse in pregnancy or postpartum is a stronger driver of poor outcomes than SSRI exposure
explanation.pearls: The two commonest errors are stopping the SSRI in T3 to avoid neonatal effects and switching to fluoxetine on habit. Both destabilise a stable patient.

sources.label: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Practice Guideline
Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Pregnancy and Lactation

stem:
A 26-year-old woman with a longstanding diagnosis of borderline personality disorder presents to a metropolitan emergency department at 11 p.m. after cutting her forearm superficially with a razor following an argument with her partner earlier this evening. The wounds are non-penetrating, have stopped bleeding after simple pressure, and do not require sutures. She has a history of six similar presentations over the past 18 months, none requiring admission.

She is engaged with a specialist BPD team and is between weekly individual dialectical behaviour therapy sessions with her regular therapist. She reports the cutting was to "stop the numb feeling" and she has no active suicidal plan or means, no current thoughts of ending her life beyond a vague chronic wish to "not exist", and she has attended tonight because her partner insisted. She is contactable, calm on interview, and denies any intent to leave against advice. She has no active psychosis, no alcohol or drug use tonight, and her regular sertraline is unchanged.

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits
data_table.Mental state: no evidence of psychosis, mood dysphoric and reactive, judgement intact, chronic passive suicidal ideation but no acute plan or means
data_table.Wound assessment: three superficial parallel lacerations to the left volar forearm, all under 2 cm, no tendon involvement, bleeding controlled with dressing

lead_in: What is the most appropriate disposition and management plan?

options.text: Admit to an acute mental health inpatient unit for observation and weekly individual dialectical behaviour therapy while an inpatient bed
options.rationale: Routine admission for self-harm in BPD is discouraged because it risks reinforcement of maladaptive coping and disrupts the community DBT frame. Structured community follow-up is preferred. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder

options.text: Detain under the state Mental Health Act for involuntary community treatment order for at least 3 months from today onwards
options.rationale: Involuntary treatment requires a treatable mental illness meeting statutory criteria and there is no evidence here that involuntary intervention is proportionate or necessary. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder

options.text: Prescribe intramuscular olanzapine 10 mg as a chemical restraint and admit to the emergency department short stay unit for the night
options.rationale: She is calm and cooperative with no agitation warranting chemical restraint, which would also breach least-restrictive practice principles. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder

options.text: Discharge home with a written safety plan, contact details for her BPD team, and next-day contact from the team to arrange early review
options.rationale: Acute chronic self-harm in BPD without evidence of acute suicidal intent, means, or intoxication is best managed with a safety plan and rapid follow-up from the specialist BPD team rather than admission. RANZCP and NHMRC BPD guidelines both emphasise that inpatient admission for chronic self-harm risks regression, iatrogenic dependence, and worsening of long-term outcomes. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder

options.text: Increase her sertraline from current dose to 200 mg daily in the emergency department as a step-up for self-harm prevention going forward
options.rationale: SSRIs are not indicated for BPD self-harm prevention and dose changes are not made in an ED without shared care planning with the treating team. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder

explanation.summary: Chronic self-harm in a person with BPD who is engaged with a specialist team and has no acute risk of completed suicide is best managed with a documented safety plan, wound care, and rapid follow-up rather than admission. The NHMRC BPD guideline explicitly cautions against reflex admission because it risks regression and dependence. Involuntary treatment requires proportionate statutory criteria that are not met here.
key_points: Chronic self-harm in BPD is not itself an indication for admission when there is no acute suicidal intent, means, or intoxication
Written safety plan with next-day contact from the specialist team is the AU standard
Involuntary treatment reserved for a defined treatable mental illness meeting statutory criteria
explanation.pearls: Distinguish chronic passive suicidality (a long-term feature of BPD) from acute suicidal intent with plan and means. The former does not justify admission; the latter does.

sources.label: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder
RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Personality Disorders

subtopic_detail: Fitness to drive on stimulant medication
stem:
A 34-year-old man is reviewed 8 weeks after commencing dexamfetamine sulfate 15 mg twice daily for newly diagnosed adult attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. He reports substantial improvement in workplace concentration and no cardiovascular symptoms. He is a private car driver only, does not hold a commercial licence, and has no history of previous crashes or driving offences. He asks whether he needs to notify the state driver licensing authority.

His blood pressure has been stable at 128/78 on treatment and his resting electrocardiogram remains normal. He has no history of substance use disorder and takes no other regular medications. He has not been advised by his psychiatrist to avoid driving. His partner and colleagues have commented that his concentration is much improved and he no longer misses turns or drifts across lanes on his commute.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 76, blood pressure 128/78, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees
data_table.Investigations: resting ECG normal with sinus rhythm and QTc 400 milliseconds

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice regarding his driving?

options.text: He does not need to notify because his symptoms are well controlled on stimulant medication and he holds only a private not commercial licence class
options.rationale: Symptom control does not remove the notification obligation. ADHD remains a notifiable condition under Austroads and the state driver licensing authority determines the licence conditions. (Source: Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive 2022)

options.text: He must cease driving entirely because stimulant medications for ADHD disqualify all patients from holding an Australian driving licence permanently
options.rationale: Stimulant medication does not automatically disqualify a driver. Austroads assesses on the underlying condition and its treatment; most well-treated adults with ADHD retain their private licence with conditions. (Source: Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive 2022)

options.text: The doctor is required to notify the state driver licensing authority on the patient's behalf without informing the patient of that decision
options.rationale: The primary obligation is on the driver. The doctor advises the patient of their notification duty and only reports directly if the patient continues to drive contrary to advice (jurisdiction-dependent mandatory reporting). (Source: Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive 2022)

options.text: He may continue driving without notification provided he keeps his blood pressure below 140/90 and undergoes an annual electrocardiogram
options.rationale: Cardiovascular monitoring is important on stimulant therapy but is separate from the licensing notification obligation for the underlying ADHD diagnosis. (Source: Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive 2022)

options.text: He is required to notify the state driver licensing authority himself, because untreated or treated ADHD may affect fitness to drive under the Austroads criteria
options.rationale: Under Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive, ADHD is a notifiable condition that may affect driving. The legal obligation to notify rests with the driver, not the doctor. The treating doctor advises about impact and reports if the driver does not notify, per state-based mandatory reporting requirements (varies by jurisdiction). (Source: Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive 2022)

explanation.summary: ADHD is a notifiable condition under Austroads and the primary obligation to notify rests with the driver, not the doctor. Most adults with well-treated ADHD retain their private licence, sometimes with conditions. Doctors must inform the patient of the notification duty and, in jurisdictions with mandatory reporting, report only if the patient continues to drive contrary to advice.
key_points: Austroads is the AU national standard for medical fitness to drive
Primary notification duty is on the driver; doctor documents advice given
Mandatory doctor reporting varies by state (e.g. NT, SA have mandatory reporting; NSW, VIC discretionary)
explanation.pearls: The two-part rule is easy to forget: it is the diagnosis that is notifiable, not the medication. Well-treated ADHD often keeps its licence.

sources.label: RANZCP Adult ADHD Clinical Practice Guideline

stem:
A 26-year-old woman with a history of schizophrenia is brought to the emergency department by her family after 4 days of progressive immobility. She sits motionless with her right arm held in an awkward flexed posture that she maintains for hours when placed by staff. She has not eaten or drunk voluntarily for 24 hours and has been echolalic when spoken to. She has no fever and no rigidity, and she does not resist passive movement of her limbs.

Her regular olanzapine 10 mg nightly has been unchanged for 12 months. She has no illicit drug use per her family and her urine drug screen is negative. Blood tests including full blood count, urea and electrolytes, calcium, creatine kinase and inflammatory markers are within normal limits. A non-contrast computed tomography scan of the brain is normal. Her creatinine is 62 micromol/L (45-90).

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 88, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees
data_table.Investigations: creatine kinase 90 U/L (less than 200), electrolytes and calcium within normal limits, non-contrast CT brain reported as normal, urine drug screen negative
data_table.Bush-Francis catatonia rating scale: screening positive with mutism, immobility, waxy flexibility, posturing, echolalia

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial diagnostic and therapeutic step?

options.text: Administer intravenous lorazepam 2 mg and observe for improvement in mutism and posturing over the following 15 to 30 minutes as a test
options.rationale: The lorazepam challenge (typically 1 to 2 mg IV) is both diagnostic and therapeutic in catatonia: at least 50 percent improvement in Bush-Francis scale features supports the diagnosis and identifies responders who benefit from a lorazepam trial as ongoing treatment. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Catatonia)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Catatonia

options.text: Increase her olanzapine dose to 20 mg nightly on the assumption that the presentation represents worsening psychotic symptoms not otherwise
options.rationale: Increasing antipsychotic dose in unrecognised catatonia risks progression to malignant catatonia and neuroleptic malignant syndrome. It is not the correct step. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Catatonia)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Catatonia

options.text: Commence subcutaneous dantrolene 1 mg/kg for suspected neuroleptic malignant syndrome pending further biochemistry results and observation
options.rationale: NMS presents with hyperthermia, rigidity, and elevated CK; none are present. The clinical picture is catatonia and dantrolene is not the initial step. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Catatonia)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Catatonia

options.text: Arrange urgent electroconvulsive therapy without any pharmacological trial because ECT is the fastest treatment for catatonia in the acute setting
options.rationale: ECT is highly effective and is escalated to when the lorazepam trial fails or catatonia becomes malignant, but a lorazepam challenge precedes ECT in most cases and provides same-day evidence to guide ongoing care. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Catatonia)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Catatonia

options.text: Perform a lumbar puncture and commence intravenous aciclovir for suspected herpes simplex encephalitis after a normal computed tomography scan
options.rationale: There is no fever, no CSF-suggestive features, and no focal neurology; the pretest probability of HSV encephalitis is very low relative to the strong catatonia phenotype. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Catatonia)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Catatonia

explanation.summary: The lorazepam challenge (1 to 2 mg IV) is the AU first-line diagnostic and therapeutic step for suspected catatonia. Response supports the diagnosis and identifies patients for ongoing lorazepam treatment. Escalating antipsychotic dose in unrecognised catatonia can precipitate malignant catatonia or NMS. ECT is second-line for lorazepam non-responders and first-line for malignant catatonia.
key_points: Bush-Francis features (mutism, posturing, waxy flexibility, echolalia) trigger the diagnostic pathway
Lorazepam 1 to 2 mg IV challenge with response at 15 to 30 minutes
Escalate to ECT if lorazepam trial fails or in malignant catatonia (hyperthermia, autonomic instability)
explanation.pearls: The absence of fever, rigidity and CK elevation separates catatonia from NMS. Both are treated by stopping the offending antipsychotic; catatonia adds lorazepam, NMS adds cooling and dantrolene.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Catatonia

stem:
A 30-year-old woman is brought to a regional emergency department 90 minutes after an intentional overdose of her partner's amitriptyline. She has taken an estimated 40 tablets of 25 mg (approximately 1000 mg total, weight 60 kg). She was found drowsy at home but is now more alert on arrival with a GCS of 13. She has no history of ischaemic heart disease and takes no other regular medications; she has occasional migraine for which she uses paracetamol.

Initial vitals show pulse rate 128 regular, blood pressure 92/56, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees. Her mucous membranes are dry. Her electrocardiogram shows sinus tachycardia at 128 with a rightward terminal R wave in lead aVR and a QRS duration of 130 milliseconds. Serum electrolytes show sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145) and potassium 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0). Serum paracetamol drawn now is 15 mg/L (treatment line 150 mg/L at 4 hours). Bedside blood glucose is 5.2 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 128, blood pressure 92/56, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees
data_table.Investigations: sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), bicarbonate 22 mmol/L (22-30), venous pH 7.34, QRS 130 milliseconds, terminal R wave in aVR positive, paracetamol level 15 mg/L (subtherapeutic)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer intravenous flumazenil 200 microgram to reverse suspected central nervous system depression from the tricyclic overdose in this case
options.rationale: Flumazenil is a benzodiazepine antagonist and has no role in TCA overdose. It risks precipitating seizures in mixed overdoses. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology - Tricyclic antidepressants)

options.text: Administer intravenous phenytoin 15 mg/kg loading dose over 30 minutes to reduce the risk of TCA-related generalised tonic-clonic seizures
options.rationale: Phenytoin is contraindicated in TCA toxicity because it worsens sodium channel blockade and is proarrhythmic. Benzodiazepines are the correct anticonvulsant here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology - Tricyclic antidepressants)

options.text: Administer intravenous sodium bicarbonate 8.4 percent 1 to 2 mmol/kg bolus and repeat as needed to target a QRS width under 100 milliseconds
options.rationale: In TCA toxicity, sodium bicarbonate is indicated when the QRS is above 100 milliseconds, there is a positive terminal R wave in aVR, ventricular arrhythmia, or hypotension unresponsive to fluid. Doses of 1 to 2 mmol/kg are given as bolus and repeated with the QRS width as the target endpoint. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology - Tricyclic antidepressants)

options.text: Administer intravenous physostigmine 2 mg to reverse the anticholinergic component of the overdose and improve mental status quickly
options.rationale: Physostigmine is contraindicated in TCA overdose because of the risk of asystole and seizures. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology - Tricyclic antidepressants)

options.text: Administer intravenous procainamide 100 mg over 5 minutes to control tachycardia and reduce the risk of ventricular arrhythmia progression
options.rationale: Class Ia antiarrhythmics worsen TCA sodium channel blockade and are contraindicated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology - Tricyclic antidepressants)

explanation.summary: TCA cardiotoxicity manifests as QRS prolongation and a terminal R wave in aVR, reflecting sodium channel blockade. Sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg IV is both alkalinising and sodium-loading, reversing the channel blockade. The dose is titrated to QRS width under 100 milliseconds. Class Ia and Ic antiarrhythmics and phenytoin are contraindicated. Benzodiazepines treat seizures; intubation and lipid emulsion are reserved for refractory instability.
key_points: Bicarbonate indications: QRS over 100 ms, terminal R in aVR, ventricular arrhythmia, hypotension not responsive to fluid
Target QRS under 100 ms and arterial pH 7.50 to 7.55 during boluses
Contraindicated: flumazenil, physostigmine, phenytoin, class Ia/Ic antiarrhythmics
explanation.pearls: The single most sensitive early ECG marker of significant TCA toxicity is the terminal R wave in aVR greater than 3 mm. It appears before the QRS widens beyond 100 ms.

subtopic_detail: Schizoaffective disorder versus bipolar with psychosis
stem:
A 24-year-old man is admitted with a 4-week episode of persecutory delusions (that ASIO is monitoring him), auditory hallucinations of a running commentary, elevated mood, and reduced need for sleep. He has had two prior similar admissions in the past 3 years. Careful longitudinal history taken from him and his father indicates that between admissions he has continued to hear intermittent voices and hold odd persecutory beliefs for approximately 4 to 6 weeks at a time without any prominent mood elevation, depression, or functional impairment beyond a mild degree.

Collateral confirms two prior manic episodes each lasting 3 to 4 weeks, each with prominent psychotic features, with full inter-episode return of mood to euthymia. He has been abstinent from cannabis and other substances for over 12 months, confirmed by urine drug screens. He has no family history of bipolar disorder. His current medication is quetiapine 400 mg nightly, tolerated well.

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits
data_table.Mental state: elevated mood, pressured speech, grandiose and persecutory delusions, third-person auditory hallucinations, no cognitive impairment
data_table.Substance use: abstinent from cannabis and other substances for over 12 months, current urine drug screen negative
data_table.Collateral: between-episode auditory hallucinations and mild persecutory beliefs persist for approximately 4 to 6 weeks after mood settles

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Bipolar I disorder with mood-congruent psychotic features because he has clear manic episodes and psychotic symptoms only during mood episodes
options.rationale: Bipolar I with psychotic features requires psychotic symptoms to be confined to mood episodes. The persistence of voices and persecutory beliefs for 4 to 6 weeks between mood episodes excludes this. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Schizophrenia because he has active phase symptoms of hallucinations and delusions with residual features between the acute admissions ongoing
options.rationale: Schizophrenia requires either mood symptoms to be absent OR the total duration of any mood episodes to be brief relative to the psychotic illness. His repeated 3 to 4 week manic episodes are prominent, not brief. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Substance/medication induced psychotic disorder because cannabis has a very high lifetime prevalence in comorbid psychotic disorders in this age group
options.rationale: He has been abstinent for over 12 months with negative urine drug screens and symptoms have persisted, so a substance-induced diagnosis is not appropriate. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Schizoaffective disorder because psychotic symptoms persist for at least 2 weeks without prominent mood symptoms during the illness course overall
options.rationale: Schizoaffective disorder (DSM-5) requires an uninterrupted illness with a mood episode concurrent with psychotic symptoms, PLUS at least 2 weeks of psychotic symptoms in the absence of a prominent mood episode. This patient's between-episode voices and delusions lasting 4 to 6 weeks meet this criterion. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Brief psychotic disorder because his episodes each last less than a month and have a spontaneous resolution back to a functioning premorbid level
options.rationale: Brief psychotic disorder requires symptoms lasting more than a day but less than a month, with full return to premorbid function. His episodes exceed a month and psychotic symptoms persist between them. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

explanation.summary: Bipolar I with psychotic features and schizoaffective disorder are separated by whether psychotic symptoms occur ONLY during mood episodes (bipolar I) or persist for at least 2 weeks in the absence of a prominent mood episode (schizoaffective). This patient's 4 to 6 weeks of between-episode auditory hallucinations and persecutory beliefs meet the schizoaffective criterion. Schizophrenia is excluded because mood episodes are not brief relative to the overall course.
key_points: Schizoaffective disorder requires greater than 2 weeks of psychotic symptoms without prominent mood symptoms during the illness course
Bipolar I with psychotic features restricts psychotic symptoms to mood episodes only
Schizophrenia allows brief mood symptoms only, not prominent recurrent manic episodes
explanation.pearls: Nail the schizoaffective diagnosis on the between-episode window. Anything under 2 weeks of psychotic symptoms without mood makes it bipolar with psychotic features; anything longer makes it schizoaffective.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Schizophrenia and Related Disorders

stem:
A 24-year-old man with first-episode psychosis has been established on olanzapine 15 mg nightly for four months. His symptoms have responded well and he has resumed his TAFE course. His weight has risen from 82 kg (BMI 26.5) at initiation to 91 kg (BMI 29.4) today.

He reports increased appetite and constant thirst but no polyuria. Baseline fasting glucose was 4.6 mmol/L and HbA1c 5.3 percent (below 5.7). He drinks alcohol two standard drinks twice a week and does not smoke. He is asking whether he should change medications.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 80/min, blood pressure 128/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Weight 91 kg; waist circumference 100 cm; no acanthosis nigricans; no proximal myopathy or striae; euthymic
data_table.Investigations: Fasting glucose 5.8 mmol/L, HbA1c 6.1 percent (below 5.7), total cholesterol 5.6 mmol/L (below 5.5), triglycerides 2.4 mmol/L (below 2.0), LDL 3.5 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next management step?

options.text: Increase olanzapine to 20 mg nightly and re-check metabolic panel in six months
options.rationale: Increasing olanzapine worsens the metabolic problem; monitoring must be more frequent than 6 monthly given the deterioration. (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Metabolic Monitoring)

options.text: Refer to dietitian only and continue current olanzapine dose without medication change
options.rationale: Dietary review alone is insufficient when olanzapine (highest metabolic risk atypical) is driving the change and HbA1c is now in prediabetes range. (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Metabolic Monitoring)

options.text: Switch to aripiprazole with cross-titration and refer for lifestyle intervention support
options.rationale: Aripiprazole has the lowest metabolic risk of common atypicals; switching alongside lifestyle intervention is RANZCP-recommended when metabolic changes emerge. (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Metabolic Monitoring)

options.text: Start metformin 500 mg twice daily and continue olanzapine at present dose
options.rationale: Metformin is adjunctive for antipsychotic weight gain but does not solve the underlying drug driver; switch is the preferred RANZCP step first. (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Metabolic Monitoring)

options.text: Cease all antipsychotic medication immediately and refer to community mental health team
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation risks psychotic relapse and is not justified when a lower-risk agent can be substituted with cross-titration. (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Metabolic Monitoring)

explanation.summary: Antipsychotic-associated metabolic risk is highest for olanzapine and clozapine, intermediate for quetiapine and risperidone, and lowest for aripiprazole, ziprasidone, and lurasidone. RANZCP monitoring includes weight and waist at every review, fasting glucose or HbA1c and lipids at baseline, 3 months, then annually (more frequently if changes emerge). When metabolic deterioration is significant and the patient is stable, cross-titration to a lower-risk agent (e.g. aripiprazole) is first-line; metformin is a second-line adjunct if switch is not possible or fails.
key_points: Olanzapine has highest metabolic risk; aripiprazole among the lowest.
Monitor weight and waist at every review, glucose and lipids at 3 months.
Switch first-line, metformin second-line for weight gain.
Never stop antipsychotic abruptly in a responder.
explanation.pearls: For olanzapine-induced weight gain with new prediabetes, cross-titrate to aripiprazole first; metformin 500 to 1000 mg BD is second-line if switching fails.

stem:
A 41-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has been on lithium carbonate 900 mg nightly for six years with excellent mood stability and no relapses. She attends for her routine annual review. Her most recent lithium level three months ago was 0.7 mmol/L (0.6 to 1.0).

She has gained 4 kg over the last year and reports feeling colder than usual, particularly in her hands. Her recent bloods show serum creatinine 92 micromol/L (baseline five years ago was 62 micromol/L), TSH 6.2 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0), free T4 within normal limits, and corrected calcium 2.68 mmol/L (2.10 to 2.60).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 62/min, blood pressure 128/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Euthymic, no tremor, no ataxia; dry skin; delayed relaxation of ankle jerks; no palpable goitre; no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Serum lithium 0.7 mmol/L; TSH 6.2 mIU/L; corrected calcium 2.68 mmol/L; PTH 8.4 pmol/L (1.6 to 6.9); creatinine 92 micromol/L; eGFR 68 mL/min/1.73 m2

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate combined next step?

options.text: Increase lithium to 1200 mg nightly targeting 0.8 to 1.0 mmol/L range for mood stability
options.rationale: Increasing lithium worsens both the renal decline and the hypercalcaemia; the patient is euthymic and does not need higher levels. (Source: RANZCP: Lithium monitoring; AMH)

options.text: Stop lithium abruptly and start sodium valproate 500 mg BD for mood stabilisation
options.rationale: Abrupt lithium cessation carries high relapse risk; sudden switches skip the tapering and mood monitoring needed. (Source: RANZCP: Lithium monitoring; AMH)

options.text: Start propranolol 20 mg twice daily for lithium-induced postural tremor management alone
options.rationale: Beta-blockers treat postural lithium tremor but do not address hypothyroidism, hypercalcaemia or renal decline. (Source: RANZCP: Lithium monitoring; AMH)

options.text: Start amiloride 5 mg daily for lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus prevention
options.rationale: Amiloride is used for established nephrogenic DI with polyuria; there is no polyuria here and other issues are more pressing. (Source: RANZCP: Lithium monitoring; AMH)

options.text: Start levothyroxine 50 micrograms daily and refer for endocrinology review of hyperparathyroidism
options.rationale: TSH 6.2 with symptoms warrants replacement; PTH 8.4 with corrected calcium 2.68 is lithium-induced primary hyperparathyroidism needing endocrine review. (Source: RANZCP: Lithium monitoring; AMH)

explanation.summary: Long-term lithium therapy causes hypothyroidism (10 to 20 percent within 5 years, higher in women), hyperparathyroidism (up to 10 percent), and progressive reduction in eGFR. RANZCP monitoring includes 6-monthly lithium level, TSH, calcium and renal function once stable. Hypothyroidism is treated with levothyroxine rather than lithium cessation; symptomatic hyperparathyroidism warrants endocrine referral (parathyroidectomy considered if severe). Progressive eGFR decline may require dose reduction, alternate day dosing, or switch to an alternative mood stabiliser after balancing relapse risk.
key_points: Lithium causes hypothyroidism, hyperparathyroidism, reduced eGFR.
6-monthly TSH, calcium, renal function once stable.
Hypothyroidism managed with levothyroxine, not lithium cessation.
Hyperparathyroidism with symptoms warrants endocrine referral.
explanation.pearls: Long-term lithium: TSH above 4 needs levothyroxine, corrected calcium above 2.60 with high PTH warrants endocrine referral; do not stop lithium unless renal decline is severe.

stem:
A 26-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder attends for annual review. She has been well controlled on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily for two years with no admissions and no depressive or manic episodes. She has recently commenced a new relationship and asks about future family planning as her partner has raised the topic.

Her last menstrual period was two weeks ago. She uses condoms currently and is not on hormonal contraception. She has been asymptomatic and prefers to remain on valproate as it has been very effective for her.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert, engaged; euthymic; no tremor or ataxia; no evidence of pregnancy
data_table.Investigations: Serum valproate 620 micromol/L (300 to 700); TSH 1.4 mIU/L; beta hCG negative today

lead_in: What is the most appropriate combined action?

options.text: Continue valproate; commence folic acid 500 micrograms daily and review annually
options.rationale: Continuing valproate in a woman of reproductive potential without highly effective contraception is contrary to TGA and MHRA requirements. (Source: TGA sodium valproate risk minimisation; MHRA Pregnancy Prevention)
source_refs: TGA Sodium Valproate Risk Minimisation Materials

options.text: Continue valproate; add copper IUD and commence folic acid 5 mg daily immediately
options.rationale: Continuing valproate remains high risk even with contraception; the TGA now requires switching in most women of reproductive potential planning conception. (Source: TGA sodium valproate risk minimisation)
source_refs: TGA Sodium Valproate Risk Minimisation Materials

options.text: Cease valproate abruptly today; commence quetiapine 50 mg BD titrating upward
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation risks relapse; cross-titration with a preconception plan is safer than sudden switching. (Source: TGA sodium valproate risk minimisation)
source_refs: TGA Sodium Valproate Risk Minimisation Materials

options.text: Refer to specialist psychiatrist for pre-conception planning and switch off valproate
options.rationale: TGA and RANZCP require valproate discontinuation planning with specialist input before conception; risks include neural tube defects (10 percent) and neurodevelopmental disorders (30 to 40 percent). (Source: TGA sodium valproate risk minimisation)
source_refs: TGA Sodium Valproate Risk Minimisation Materials

options.text: Halve valproate to 500 mg daily and add lamotrigine 25 mg to prepare for conception
options.rationale: Even reduced-dose valproate carries substantial teratogenic and neurodevelopmental risk; incomplete switching does not remove the exposure hazard. (Source: TGA sodium valproate risk minimisation)
source_refs: TGA Sodium Valproate Risk Minimisation Materials

explanation.summary: Valproate exposure in pregnancy causes a 10 percent risk of major congenital malformation (particularly neural tube defects) and 30 to 40 percent risk of neurodevelopmental disorders in exposed children. TGA now requires acknowledged discussion, use of highly effective contraception, and specialist review before use in women of reproductive potential. Pre-conception, the plan is switch to a lower-risk mood stabiliser (lamotrigine, quetiapine, sometimes lithium after individual risk-benefit) with careful cross-titration over months. Folic acid 5 mg daily is added if valproate cannot be avoided. Postpartum medication planning includes breastfeeding compatibility (valproate is compatible if used, but the goal is avoidance).
key_points: Valproate NTD risk 10 percent, neurodevelopmental 30 to 40 percent.
TGA requires contraception documentation and specialist review.
Pre-conception switch to lamotrigine or quetiapine over months.
Folic acid 5 mg daily if valproate unavoidable.
explanation.pearls: Any woman of reproductive potential on valproate needs specialist pre-conception planning and switch to lamotrigine or quetiapine; 10 percent NTD risk is not modifiable by folic acid alone.

sources.label: TGA Sodium Valproate Risk Minimisation Materials

stem:
A 27-year-old woman presents to a GP saying that she thinks she may have ADHD after her nephew was recently diagnosed. She reports lifelong difficulty finishing tasks, losing keys and wallet, chronic lateness, and needing to reread paragraphs. She dropped out of university in second year and has changed jobs six times.

She has no history of substance use, no mood disorder currently, and no previous psychiatric admissions. She holds a manual car licence and commutes 45 minutes to work daily. Her PHQ-9 today is 6 and GAD-7 is 5. She asks whether she can start medication urgently.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 80/min, blood pressure 122/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert, engaged; no thought disorder; euthymic; no tics or motor abnormalities
data_table.Investigations: PHQ-9 6, GAD-7 5, ASRS-6 positive on 5 of 6 items; TSH 1.6 mIU/L; ferritin 48 mcg/L; iron studies within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Trial atomoxetine 40 mg oral daily now under the GP; review at four weeks
options.rationale: Atomoxetine can be initiated by GP under an authority prescription only for confirmed ADHD; diagnosis has not yet been made. (Source: RACGP; RANZCP ADHD Guideline)

options.text: Refer to a psychiatrist for structured adult ADHD assessment before any medication trial
options.rationale: Adult ADHD diagnosis in AU requires psychiatrist assessment for stimulant authorisation; GP self-management is not permitted first-line. (Source: RANZCP Adult ADHD Guideline; state stimulant authority rules)

options.text: Trial methylphenidate immediate release 10 mg BD from the GP with driving advice
options.rationale: Stimulants require state-based authority prescriber (usually psychiatrist) for adult initiation; GP alone cannot start. (Source: RANZCP Adult ADHD Guideline)

options.text: Recommend cognitive behavioural therapy alone for eight sessions before considering medication
options.rationale: CBT is a helpful adjunct but should not delay assessment and treatment when functional impairment is established. (Source: RANZCP Adult ADHD Guideline)

options.text: Advise this is likely age-appropriate distractibility; reassure and review in six months
options.rationale: Reassurance in the presence of impairment across educational, occupational and daily life domains misses a diagnosable condition. (Source: RANZCP Adult ADHD Guideline)

explanation.summary: Adult ADHD in Australia requires psychiatrist (or paediatrician for those under 18) assessment for diagnosis and stimulant authorisation. GP shared care can continue treatment once initiated. Assessment includes DSM-5 criteria (five of nine inattentive or hyperactive-impulsive symptoms persisting over 6 months with impairment in more than one setting, onset before age 12 by history), collateral where possible, and comorbid mood, anxiety, learning disorder screening. Treatment options include long-acting methylphenidate or lisdexamfetamine; atomoxetine and guanfacine are non-stimulant options. Driving advice: patients must self-report medical conditions affecting driving; stimulants generally improve driving safety once titrated, but untreated ADHD is associated with elevated crash risk.
key_points: Adult ADHD diagnosis by psychiatrist required for stimulants in AU.
GP shared care after psychiatrist initiation.
Onset before age 12 by history required for DSM-5.
Driving safer with treated than untreated ADHD.
explanation.pearls: For suspected adult ADHD, refer to a psychiatrist first; state stimulant authorities preclude GP-only initiation, but GP shared care can continue treatment once established.

stem:
A 28-year-old man with schizoaffective disorder is brought to ED by family after four days of progressive withdrawal, mutism, and staying frozen in unusual postures. On the ward he has been observed to hold an arm in mid-air after physical positioning by the nurse and repeats phrases spoken to him. He has not eaten or drunk in 36 hours.

He was on aripiprazole 15 mg daily until two weeks ago when he self-ceased. He has had no antipsychotics since. His mother reports he had a similar episode two years ago that resolved with ECT after an unsuccessful medication trial.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108/min, blood pressure 108/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 37.1 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Mute, waxy flexibility on limb positioning, echolalia, staring; no rigidity or tremor; no autonomic instability
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 320 U/L (below 200); electrolytes within normal limits; venous blood gas within normal limits; CT brain normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate diagnostic and initial treatment step?

options.text: Recommence aripiprazole 30 mg oral daily targeting rapid remission of psychosis
options.rationale: Antipsychotics can worsen catatonia and precipitate neuroleptic malignant syndrome; benzodiazepine challenge first. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; RANZCP catatonia)

options.text: Commence olanzapine 10 mg intramuscular now for rapid tranquillisation of psychosis
options.rationale: IM antipsychotic risks precipitating NMS in catatonia; guideline sequence is lorazepam challenge then ECT if refractory. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Give lorazepam 1 to 2 mg intravenous or intramuscular as a diagnostic and therapeutic challenge
options.rationale: Lorazepam challenge is diagnostic and therapeutic; a 50 percent reduction in catatonia score within 10 minutes confirms diagnosis and guides therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; RANZCP)

options.text: Refer for emergent ECT under a mental health treatment order today as first therapy
options.rationale: ECT is next-line if lorazepam challenge fails or in malignant catatonia; a lorazepam trial precedes it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Start haloperidol 5 mg oral three times daily and clonazepam 0.5 mg BD together
options.rationale: Haloperidol has the highest NMS risk in catatonia; combination with benzodiazepine does not offset that risk. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Catatonia may present in schizophrenia, mood disorders, delirium, autoimmune encephalitis and other medical conditions. The lorazepam challenge (1 to 2 mg IV or IM) is diagnostic and therapeutic: a marked reduction in Bush Francis Catatonia Rating Scale within 10 minutes confirms diagnosis and guides ongoing treatment (typically lorazepam 2 mg three or four times daily). If two adequate benzodiazepine trials fail, ECT is the next step (also first-line if malignant catatonia with autonomic instability). Antipsychotics can worsen catatonia and precipitate NMS, so they are held during acute treatment.
key_points: Lorazepam 1 to 2 mg IV or IM as challenge test.
50 percent BFCRS reduction confirms diagnosis.
ECT is next-line if benzodiazepines fail.
Withhold antipsychotics acutely to avoid NMS.
explanation.pearls: Suspected catatonia: give lorazepam 1 to 2 mg IV; a rapid response within 10 minutes both confirms diagnosis and treats it, and antipsychotics should be held meanwhile.

stem:
A 35-year-old man is admitted after his third manic episode with psychotic features. On this admission he had elated mood, reduced sleep for a week, grandiose delusions and pressured speech; symptoms resolved within four weeks of olanzapine and mood stabilisation. His two prior episodes were similar and both resolved with treatment.

Between episodes over the past four years he has held a stable job and had good functional recovery. Records show three months of persistent auditory hallucinations after his first admission before eventually resolving during a period of no mood symptoms. He is not currently symptomatic.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76/min, blood pressure 122/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert, engaged, euthymic; no formal thought disorder currently; no active psychosis on interview
data_table.Investigations: TSH 1.8 mIU/L (within normal limits); serum lithium 0.8 mmol/L (0.6 to 1.0); urine drug screen negative; MRI brain normal

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Schizoaffective disorder bipolar type, requiring lifetime mood and antipsychotic combination therapy
options.rationale: Psychosis persisting for two weeks or more outside a mood episode plus mood episodes with psychotic features across illness course meets DSM-5 schizoaffective bipolar type criteria. (Source: DSM-5-TR; RANZCP Bipolar Guidelines)

options.text: Bipolar I disorder with mood congruent psychotic features during the manic episodes only
options.rationale: Bipolar I with psychotic features requires psychosis to be confined to mood episodes; three months of psychosis without mood symptoms excludes this. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Schizophrenia with superimposed mood episodes secondary to reactive depression from illness
options.rationale: Schizophrenia excludes schizoaffective when full mood episodes are present for the majority of illness course; a mood episode dominates here. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Substance-induced mood disorder with psychotic features from prior methamphetamine use
options.rationale: Urine drug screen is negative and episodes recur without substance use; this is not substance induced. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Brief psychotic disorder with recurrent depression and mania as separate mood diagnoses
options.rationale: Brief psychotic disorder requires duration less than one month; three months of psychosis excludes this. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

explanation.summary: Schizoaffective disorder requires: (a) an uninterrupted period of illness during which a major mood episode co-occurs with schizophrenia criterion A symptoms; (b) delusions or hallucinations for two or more weeks in the absence of a major mood episode during the lifetime course; (c) mood episodes present for the majority of the total duration of illness (differentiates from schizophrenia); and (d) not attributable to a substance or medical condition. Bipolar type has manic episodes; depressive type has only depression. Management includes long-term mood stabiliser plus antipsychotic (typically lithium plus olanzapine or aripiprazole).
key_points: Schizoaffective needs 2+ weeks of psychosis without mood symptoms in lifetime.
Mood episodes must dominate illness course to differentiate from schizophrenia.
Bipolar type has mania; depressive type only has depression.
Treatment combines mood stabiliser plus antipsychotic.
explanation.pearls: The DSM-5 marker for schizoaffective versus bipolar with psychotic features is 2 weeks or more of psychosis outside any mood episode over the lifetime illness course.

sources.label: RANZCP: Bipolar disorder clinical practice guidelines

stem:
A 34-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia has been stable on clozapine 400 mg at night for 18 months. He was admitted to a medical ward 3 days ago with community-acquired pneumonia and clozapine was withheld throughout that admission. He is now afebrile on oral antibiotics, medically stable, and has returned to the mental health unit today. He has had no seizures. His last blood monitoring 6 weeks ago showed a neutrophil count in the green range.

He is settled without acute psychotic symptoms, sleeps well and eats normal meals. He is smoking again on the unit balcony.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82/min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert, oriented; no chest signs on auscultation; no meningism
data_table.Investigations: FBC neutrophils 3.4 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5), platelets 210 x10^9/L; CRP 22 mg/L (<5); ECG QTc 420 ms; clozapine last dose 72 hours ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate approach to restarting clozapine?

options.text: Restart clozapine at the previous maintenance dose of 400 mg orally at night tonight
options.rationale: Any interruption of clozapine of 48 hours or more requires retitration from a low starting dose (typically 12.5 to 25 mg); resuming full dose risks hypotension, cardiac collapse and myocarditis. (Source: Clozapine RCM protocol; RANZCP)

options.text: Restart clozapine at 12.5 mg orally at night and retitrate over 1 to 2 weeks
options.rationale: Any clozapine break of 48 hours or more mandates restart from 12.5 mg with slow retitration (usually 25 mg then 50 mg over subsequent days), monitoring BP and pulse; abrupt full-dose resumption is contraindicated. (Source: Clozapine RCM protocol; RANZCP)

options.text: Restart clozapine at 200 mg orally as a single dose tonight then reassess tomorrow
options.rationale: 200 mg exceeds the safe restart threshold after a 48-hour or longer break; hypotension and QTc effects are unpredictable at this dose after washout. (Source: Clozapine RCM protocol; RANZCP)

options.text: Switch to oral olanzapine 20 mg nightly and cease clozapine permanently now
options.rationale: Clozapine is definitive treatment for treatment-resistant schizophrenia; permanent cessation for a temporary medical interruption is not indicated. (Source: Clozapine RCM protocol; RANZCP)

options.text: Delay restart until FBC monitoring is repeated and the C-reactive protein normalises
options.rationale: Neutrophils are in the green range and CRP does not preclude restart; delay increases relapse risk when retitration can safely begin. (Source: Clozapine RCM protocol; RANZCP)

explanation.summary: Clozapine has a narrow therapeutic index and rapid loss of tolerance to hypotensive, cardiac and sedative effects. Any interruption of 48 hours or more requires restart at 12.5 mg with slow retitration over 1 to 2 weeks. Smoking induces CYP1A2 and lowers clozapine levels; smoking cessation during admission raises levels and dose reduction is often needed on quitting. Weekly full blood count monitoring restarts at the beginning of retitration (or aligns with local Clozapine Patient Monitoring Service requirements). Cardiac monitoring including ECG for QTc and troponin for myocarditis surveillance is undertaken over the first weeks.
key_points: Interruption 48 hours or more requires restart at 12.5 mg.
Retitration typically 12.5, 25, 50 mg over days.
Smoking induces CYP1A2; ceasing to smoke raises clozapine levels.
Weekly FBC monitoring restarts with retitration.
explanation.pearls: After any clozapine break of 48 hours or more, restart at 12.5 mg regardless of previous stable dose; a full-dose restart risks hypotension, sedation and myocarditis.

stem:
A 62-year-old woman on lithium carbonate 750 mg nightly for bipolar I disorder for 12 years presents with 3 days of coarse tremor, worsening confusion, unsteady gait and vomiting. She started a thiazide diuretic 2 weeks ago for hypertension. Her last outpatient lithium level 6 weeks ago was 0.7 mmol/L. On examination she is drowsy, moves all four limbs but is ataxic, and has hyperreflexia and myoclonic jerks.

She has no fever and no rash. She lives alone and has been unable to keep down water. Her partner brought her to hospital when she became confused overnight.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 37.2 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, GCS 13; coarse tremor and myoclonus; ataxic gait; brisk reflexes without clonus; dry mucous membranes
data_table.Investigations: Serum lithium 3.6 mmol/L (0.4-1.0); creatinine 168 micromol/L (60-110) up from 82 baseline; sodium 148 mmol/L (135-145); ECG QTc 470 ms; no ischaemic changes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Cease lithium and give intravenous 0.9 percent sodium chloride at 200 mL/hour alone
options.rationale: IV fluids and lithium cessation are essential but insufficient alone at this level and with neurotoxicity and renal impairment; haemodialysis is required. (Source: Australian eTG: Toxicology - Lithium)

options.text: Give activated charcoal 50 g orally and observe with 4-hourly lithium concentrations
options.rationale: Charcoal does not bind lithium; it has no role in decontamination for chronic lithium toxicity. (Source: Australian eTG: Toxicology - Lithium)

options.text: Arrange urgent haemodialysis and cease lithium with concurrent intravenous fluids
options.rationale: Haemodialysis is indicated for lithium level over 2.5 mmol/L with symptoms, level over 4 mmol/L regardless, or level over 2.5 mmol/L with renal impairment; this patient meets criteria. (Source: Australian eTG: Toxicology - Lithium; EXTRIP guidelines)

options.text: Continue lithium at half the previous dose after starting intravenous rehydration
options.rationale: Continuing lithium at any dose during acute toxicity is unsafe; the drug must be withheld. (Source: Australian eTG: Toxicology - Lithium)

options.text: Give whole bowel irrigation with polyethylene glycol until effluent runs clear now
options.rationale: Whole bowel irrigation is considered for acute massive ingestion of sustained-release preparations; not helpful in chronic toxicity from routine dosing. (Source: Australian eTG: Toxicology - Lithium)

explanation.summary: Chronic lithium toxicity is common in patients on long-term therapy after a new nephrotoxic or diuretic medication, dehydration, or intercurrent illness. Haemodialysis is indicated for lithium concentration over 4 mmol/L regardless of symptoms, or over 2.5 mmol/L with severe neurological features, renal impairment or haemodynamic instability, or when levels are expected to remain elevated for a prolonged period. Charcoal does not bind lithium. Whole bowel irrigation may be considered for acute massive sustained-release ingestion. Rebound rises in lithium after dialysis are common; extended sessions or repeat dialysis are often required.
key_points: Dialysis indicated: level over 4 always; over 2.5 with symptoms or AKI.
Chronic toxicity often precipitated by dehydration, NSAID, ACEi, thiazide.
Charcoal does not bind lithium.
Rebound rise post-dialysis is common; extended or repeat sessions needed.
explanation.pearls: For a chronic lithium toxicity patient on a thiazide with level over 2.5 mmol/L, neurotoxicity and rising creatinine, arrange urgent haemodialysis; do not just fluid-resuscitate.

subtopic_detail: Valproate in a woman planning pregnancy
stem:
A 29-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has been stable on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily for 4 years without relapse. She reports today that she and her partner are planning to start trying for a pregnancy in the next 3 months. She has a body mass index of 26, no other medical problems and does not smoke. Her last mood episode was a manic episode requiring inpatient admission 4 years ago.

She is euthymic today with no psychotic features. Her current supports are strong and she is engaged with a private psychiatrist and general practitioner.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76/min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert, euthymic; mental state examination unremarkable; no acute risk features
data_table.Investigations: TSH within normal limits; beta-hCG negative today; LFTs within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate mood-stabiliser change?

options.text: Continue valproate at current dose and arrange preconception folate supplementation
options.rationale: Valproate is highly teratogenic (neural tube defects, cardiac and skeletal defects, neurodevelopmental effects); it is contraindicated in women planning pregnancy where alternatives exist. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Psychiatry Guidelines)

options.text: Reduce valproate to 500 mg daily and add high-dose folate 5 mg daily orally
options.rationale: Dose reduction does not eliminate teratogenicity; high-dose folate does not neutralise valproate neural tube defect risk. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Psychiatry Guidelines)

options.text: Cross-taper to lithium carbonate with monitoring of levels, thyroid and renal function
options.rationale: Lithium is the safest mood stabiliser in pregnancy planning after valproate cessation, with the smallest absolute teratogenicity signal (Ebstein anomaly around 1 in 1000 to 2000) and strong evidence for bipolar prevention. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Psychiatry Guidelines)

options.text: Cross-taper to carbamazepine 200 mg twice daily with slow monthly dose titration
options.rationale: Carbamazepine is also teratogenic (neural tube defects, craniofacial malformations, developmental delay); it does not solve the problem. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Psychiatry Guidelines)

options.text: Cease valproate now with no replacement and monitor for relapse with therapy alone
options.rationale: Ceasing mood stabiliser without replacement in bipolar I with prior severe manic episode carries very high relapse risk; a replacement is essential. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Psychiatry Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Sodium valproate is contraindicated in women of childbearing potential planning pregnancy because of teratogenicity (roughly 10 percent risk of major congenital malformations including neural tube defects, and a well-documented neurodevelopmental effect). Australian guidelines require pregnancy prevention programs if valproate is unavoidable. For a woman with bipolar I disorder planning pregnancy, lithium is generally the safest evidence-based mood stabiliser: teratogenicity risk (Ebstein anomaly) is smaller than previously estimated at around 1 in 1000 to 2000, and its efficacy for relapse prevention is strong. Cross-tapering is done gradually to maintain stability, with regular level monitoring in pregnancy and postpartum dose adjustment.
key_points: Valproate is contraindicated in women planning pregnancy where alternatives exist.
Carbamazepine is also teratogenic; it is not an acceptable substitute.
Lithium is the safest bipolar mood stabiliser in pregnancy planning.
Ebstein anomaly with lithium is around 1 in 1000 to 2000, not 1 in 100.
explanation.pearls: In a woman with bipolar I disorder planning pregnancy on valproate, cross-taper to lithium; do not switch to carbamazepine and do not just reduce the valproate dose.
