stem:
A 24-year-old woman is brought to ED by ambulance 90 minutes after ingesting an estimated 60 tablets of her father's amitriptyline 50 mg. She is drowsy but responsive to voice, with a widened pulse pressure and cool peripheries. Her Glasgow Coma Score is 12. Ambulance ECG en route showed a broad QRS complex.

She has a documented depressive disorder and current suicidality was declared to the paramedics. IV access has been established and 500 mL of normal saline has been infused during transport.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128/min, blood pressure 92/56 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy, GCS 12, dry mucous membranes, dilated pupils; abdomen soft; no focal neurological deficit
data_table.Investigations: ECG QRS 132 ms, QT 460 ms, sinus tachycardia; venous gas pH 7.30, HCO3 18 mmol/L, lactate 3.2 mmol/L; paracetamol level pending; serum tricyclic assay pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Intravenous flumazenil 0.2 mg to reverse suspected co-ingestion of benzodiazepines
options.rationale: Flumazenil is contraindicated in mixed overdose because it can precipitate seizures, which are dangerous in TCA toxicity due to acidosis lowering seizure threshold. (Source: Australian eTG: Toxicology - TCA)

options.text: Oral activated charcoal 50 g and 4-hourly repeat ECG until QRS returns to normal
options.rationale: Airway is at risk in a drowsy patient; oral charcoal without intubation risks aspiration. IV therapy is required now for the widened QRS. (Source: Australian eTG: Toxicology - TCA)

options.text: Intravenous phenytoin 15 mg/kg loading dose to shorten the widened QRS
options.rationale: Phenytoin is not first-line for TCA-associated arrhythmia; sodium bicarbonate is the antidote and phenytoin can prolong QT. (Source: Australian eTG: Toxicology - TCA)

options.text: Intravenous 8.4 percent sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg bolus for the widened QRS
options.rationale: QRS over 100 ms in TCA overdose is an indication for sodium bicarbonate to correct acidosis, increase sodium load and offset sodium channel blockade; the goal is QRS narrowing and pH 7.45 to 7.55. (Source: Australian eTG: Toxicology - TCA)

options.text: Intravenous intralipid 20 percent 1.5 mL/kg bolus over one minute now empirically
options.rationale: Intralipid is reserved for cardiovascular collapse refractory to bicarbonate; first-line is sodium bicarbonate for QRS widening. (Source: Australian eTG: Toxicology - TCA)

explanation.summary: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose causes sodium channel blockade producing QRS widening, hypotension and ventricular arrhythmias, together with anticholinergic and central depressant effects. Indications for sodium bicarbonate include QRS over 100 ms, ventricular arrhythmia, or hypotension not responding to fluids. Dose is 1 to 2 mmol/kg IV boluses with the goal of narrowing QRS and reaching arterial pH 7.45 to 7.55. Airway protection is often required as GCS falls. Intralipid is second-line for refractory cardiovascular collapse. Flumazenil is contraindicated in mixed overdoses because it lowers the seizure threshold.
key_points: QRS over 100 ms in TCA overdose triggers sodium bicarbonate.
Target arterial pH 7.45 to 7.55 with bicarb boluses.
Flumazenil contraindicated; may provoke seizures.
Intralipid is reserved for refractory cardiovascular collapse.
explanation.pearls: In amitriptyline overdose, look at the QRS: over 100 ms means give sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg immediately and repeat until QRS narrows and pH is 7.45 to 7.55.

stem:
A 38-year-old man with schizophrenia has been on olanzapine 20 mg nightly for 12 weeks after an inpatient admission for a psychotic relapse. His weight at commencement was 82 kg and today at community follow-up he weighs 91 kg. He has developed increased thirst and polyuria over the past 3 weeks. He otherwise reports good mood, no psychotic features, and has been adherent.

He smokes half a pack of cigarettes a day, drinks alcohol only socially and has no personal history of diabetes. His father has type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84/min, blood pressure 138/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: BMI 29.2; acanthosis nigricans absent; no focal neurological findings
data_table.Investigations: Random glucose 12.8 mmol/L; fasting glucose (deferred but pending); HbA1c 7.2 percent; lipids: total cholesterol 6.4 mmol/L, LDL 4.2 mmol/L, HDL 0.9 mmol/L, triglycerides 3.6 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management step now?

options.text: Continue olanzapine unchanged and give dietary and exercise advice at review today
options.rationale: New-onset diabetes on olanzapine warrants a change or dose reduction of the offending agent alongside diabetes treatment; lifestyle alone will not offset the drug-induced metabolic effects. (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Metabolic Monitoring Guidelines)

options.text: Ask the patient to reduce olanzapine to 10 mg nightly with monthly HbA1c monitoring
options.rationale: Halving the dose maintains high metabolic burden; switching to a lower-risk antipsychotic (aripiprazole) is preferred when new diabetes emerges. (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Metabolic Monitoring Guidelines)

options.text: Cease olanzapine tonight without a replacement and offer clozapine within the week
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation risks psychotic relapse; clozapine is reserved for treatment-resistant illness and has its own metabolic burden. (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Metabolic Monitoring Guidelines)

options.text: Start metformin 500 mg twice daily and continue olanzapine at the current dose
options.rationale: Adding metformin without addressing the causative drug leaves ongoing metabolic drive; guideline-preferred approach is to switch the antipsychotic and manage diabetes alongside. (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Metabolic Monitoring Guidelines)

options.text: Cross-taper to aripiprazole, start metformin and refer to diabetes clinic for review
options.rationale: Guideline-preferred approach is to switch from a high metabolic risk antipsychotic (olanzapine, clozapine, quetiapine) to a lower-risk agent (aripiprazole, ziprasidone), start metformin, and coordinate with diabetes services. (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Metabolic Monitoring Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Second-generation antipsychotics vary substantially in metabolic risk. Olanzapine and clozapine are the highest-risk agents for weight gain, dyslipidaemia and new-onset diabetes; quetiapine is moderate; aripiprazole, ziprasidone and lurasidone are lowest. When metabolic complications emerge, guideline management is to cross-taper to a lower-risk agent while maintaining psychiatric stability, treat the metabolic disorder in parallel (metformin for new diabetes, statin for dyslipidaemia, blood pressure control), and continue metabolic monitoring at least every 3 months. Baseline and 3-monthly weight, waist circumference, blood pressure, fasting glucose or HbA1c, and lipids are recommended.
key_points: Olanzapine and clozapine are highest metabolic risk.
New diabetes warrants switch to lower-risk antipsychotic, not just adjunct.
Aripiprazole, ziprasidone are lowest metabolic risk.
Metabolic monitoring at baseline and 3-monthly.
explanation.pearls: When a patient on olanzapine develops new diabetes, cross-taper to aripiprazole and start metformin; do not just add metformin and continue olanzapine at full dose.

stem:
A 52-year-old man with bipolar I disorder has been maintained on lithium carbonate 900 mg nocte for 18 years with excellent mood control and no admissions in the last decade. He also takes atorvastatin 20 mg for hypercholesterolaemia. His lithium level 3 months ago was 0.7 mmol/L (0.6-1.0). His eGFR has declined progressively: 78 mL/min/1.73 m2 four years ago, 62 two years ago, and 48 today.

He is asymptomatic and works full-time. He has no polyuria, oedema or dyspnoea. Blood pressure and urinary sediment are normal. Urine albumin/creatinine ratio is 1.5 mg/mmol. He is anxious about changing his medication because his last three relapses on other agents required hospital admission. He has never taken sodium valproate and previously failed carbamazepine.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72/min, blood pressure 124/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert, oriented, euthymic mood, no thought disorder, no tremor, no ataxia
data_table.Investigations: Lithium level 0.7 mmol/L (0.6-1.0); eGFR 48 mL/min/1.73 m2 (progressive fall from 78); serum creatinine 128 micromol/L (60-110); urine albumin/creatinine 1.5 mg/mmol; TSH within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his medication management?

options.text: Reduce lithium to 450 mg nocte in the community and target a serum level of 0.4 mmol/L
options.rationale: Sub-therapeutic lithium levels risk relapse without necessarily arresting renal decline; specialist joint review is required before dose reduction. (Source: RANZCP bipolar disorder guideline)

options.text: Continue current dose unchanged and repeat renal function testing again in 12 months
options.rationale: Watching an eGFR that has fallen 30 mL/min over 4 years risks reaching dialysis-dependent CKD; specialist review is warranted now, not deferred a year. (Source: RANZCP bipolar disorder guideline)

options.text: Refer to renal and psychiatric services to plan a slow lithium taper and alternative selection
options.rationale: Progressive decline to CKD stage 3b (eGFR 48) with a rate that suggests lithium nephrotoxicity warrants joint psychiatric-renal review before further decline compromises future options. (Source: RANZCP bipolar disorder guideline)

options.text: Ceasing lithium abruptly to arrest the fall in renal function and starting oral olanzapine
options.rationale: Abrupt lithium cessation carries high relapse risk within 6 months; any change requires slow taper over months with cover from a well-planned alternative. (Source: RANZCP bipolar disorder guideline)

options.text: Add amiloride 5 mg daily to preserve renal tubular function without stopping lithium therapy
options.rationale: Amiloride helps lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, not chronic interstitial nephropathy; it does not address progressive CKD in this scenario. (Source: RANZCP bipolar disorder guideline)

explanation.summary: Chronic lithium therapy (typically over 10 years) causes chronic tubulointerstitial nephropathy in a subset of patients, presenting as slowly progressive CKD. Once eGFR falls below 60 mL/min/1.73 m2, joint renal and psychiatric review is recommended; below 45 the risk of dialysis dependence rises and lithium should usually be tapered under psychiatric guidance with an alternative mood stabiliser. Alternatives after lithium failure or intolerance include sodium valproate (avoid in women of childbearing age), lamotrigine (better for bipolar depression), quetiapine, or olanzapine, tailored to the individual. Abrupt lithium cessation causes rebound mania and should always be avoided; taper over at least 4 weeks.
key_points: Long-term lithium can cause chronic interstitial nephropathy.
eGFR under 60: joint renal and psychiatric planning.
eGFR under 45: usually taper lithium with alternative cover.
Never stop lithium abruptly; rebound mania is a real risk.
explanation.pearls: Progressive fall in eGFR to 48 in an 18-year lithium user needs specialist psych/renal referral for a planned slow taper and alternative agent; abrupt cessation causes rebound mania within 6 months.

subtopic_detail: Smoking cessation pharmacotherapy in a depression comorbidity
stem:
A 48-year-old man presents to your general practice wanting to quit smoking. He smokes 20 cigarettes a day, has smoked since age 18, and has failed two prior quit attempts using patches alone. He has a history of moderate major depressive disorder currently well controlled on sertraline 100 mg daily for 2 years. He has no history of cardiovascular disease, no seizure history and no active suicidal ideation.

He drinks alcohol socially (5 standard drinks a week). His BMI is 27 kg/m2 and his blood pressure is 132/82. He has never used bupropion or varenicline. He asks for the option most likely to help him quit for good this time.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, blood pressure 132/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert, euthymic; no clubbing; chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Recent fasting lipids and BSL within normal limits; PHQ-9 = 4

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Fluoxetine 20 mg daily instead of sertraline to help both mood and smoking cessation as the sole intervention
options.rationale: SSRIs are not evidence-based smoking cessation agents; his depression is already well controlled on sertraline. (Source: RACGP Supporting smoking cessation)

options.text: E-cigarettes (vaping) as monotherapy from the local vape store without prescriber involvement as the sole intervention
options.rationale: AU regulation of nicotine e-cigarettes now requires prescription and TGA-regulated products; unregulated vaping is not first-line pharmacotherapy. (Source: RACGP Supporting smoking cessation)

options.text: Varenicline titration starting at 0.5 mg once daily for 3 days, then 0.5 mg twice daily for 4 days, then 1 mg twice daily for 12 weeks
options.rationale: RACGP smoking cessation guidance places varenicline as first-line pharmacotherapy for adults; safety in stable depression is now well established. (Source: RACGP Supporting smoking cessation)

options.text: Bupropion sustained-release 150 mg once daily titrated to twice daily as sole pharmacotherapy as the sole intervention
options.rationale: Bupropion is an alternative but is contraindicated in seizure risk and less effective than varenicline; it is not preferred when varenicline is available. (Source: RACGP Supporting smoking cessation)

options.text: Nicotine 21 mg/24 hour patch alone applied daily without any oral pharmacotherapy as the sole intervention
options.rationale: Single-agent NRT has failed twice previously; escalation to varenicline or combination NRT is indicated. (Source: RACGP Supporting smoking cessation)

explanation.summary: The RACGP smoking cessation guideline uses the 5As framework and recommends behavioural support plus pharmacotherapy for adults smoking daily who want to quit. First-line pharmacotherapies are varenicline, combination NRT (patch plus a short-acting form) or bupropion; head-to-head evidence favours varenicline for quit rates, with combination NRT as a close second option. Varenicline safety in stable depression is now supported by the EAGLES trial data. Bupropion is contraindicated in seizure disorders, eating disorders, and MAOI use. Behavioural support (Quitline referral, motivational interviewing) is recommended alongside pharmacotherapy.
key_points: Varenicline is first-line pharmacotherapy for smoking cessation in Australian guidance.
Combination NRT is a close second when varenicline is unsuitable.
Bupropion is contraindicated in seizure risk and eating disorders.
Varenicline is safe in stable depression per EAGLES data.
explanation.pearls: For an adult smoking 20 a day who has failed NRT alone and has stable well-controlled depression, varenicline titrated to 1 mg twice daily for 12 weeks is first-line and does not require SSRI change.

stem:
A 24-year-old woman with a 2-year history of schizoaffective disorder is brought to the psychiatric emergency service by her family after 5 days of progressive mutism and reduced oral intake. She now stares fixedly ahead, does not respond to verbal prompts, and holds her arm in the position you passively place it (waxy flexibility). She is not on any antipsychotic due to an admission gap. Family report no recent illicit drug use and no fever at home.

On examination she is afebrile with normal vital signs, no rigidity beyond the posturing described, normal reflexes and no clonus. Her serum CK is 220 U/L (55-170), U and E are within normal limits, BSL 5.2 mmol/L. A CT head performed on arrival is unremarkable. Her Bush Francis Catatonia Rating Scale on admission is 16.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Mute; catalepsy with waxy flexibility; fixed gaze; no rigidity; deep tendon reflexes normal; no clonus
data_table.Investigations: CK 220 U/L (55-170); U and E within normal limits; BSL 5.2 mmol/L; CT head unremarkable; Bush Francis 16

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Load with IV valproate 20 mg/kg to address the mood component of her schizoaffective disorder
options.rationale: Valproate is a mood-stabiliser and is not a first-line treatment for catatonia. (Source: RANZCP Position Statement Catatonia)

options.text: Recommend ECT commencement within 48 hours without a benzodiazepine challenge first
options.rationale: ECT is highly effective in catatonia but is second-line after lorazepam trial when timing allows; lorazepam is safer to trial first. (Source: RANZCP Position Statement Catatonia)

options.text: Withhold treatment and observe for 48 hours to determine spontaneous resolution first
options.rationale: Untreated catatonia carries risks of DVT, pressure injuries, dehydration and progression to malignant catatonia; treatment is not delayed. (Source: RANZCP Position Statement Catatonia)

options.text: Give IV lorazepam 2 mg with observation for 10 minutes and repeat if no partial response
options.rationale: The lorazepam challenge (1-2 mg IV or IM) is diagnostic and therapeutic in catatonia and is first-line management before considering ECT. (Source: RANZCP Position Statement Catatonia; Australian eTG Psychotropic)

options.text: Load with IV haloperidol 5 mg to break the presumed psychotic stupor immediately
options.rationale: Antipsychotics can worsen catatonia and precipitate NMS; benzodiazepines are first-line. (Source: RANZCP Position Statement Catatonia)

explanation.summary: Catatonia is a syndrome characterised by mutism, immobility, posturing, waxy flexibility, negativism and stereotypy. The Bush Francis Catatonia Rating Scale supports diagnosis. The first-line intervention is the lorazepam challenge: 1 to 2 mg IV or IM lorazepam produces partial or full response in around 80 percent within an hour if catatonia is confirmed. This is both diagnostic and therapeutic. Antipsychotics can worsen catatonia and precipitate malignant catatonia or NMS and should be avoided or withdrawn during acute treatment.
key_points: First-line is a lorazepam challenge 1-2 mg IV or IM.
Antipsychotics can worsen catatonia and are avoided in the acute phase.
ECT is second-line if lorazepam fails or in malignant catatonia.
Supportive care (DVT prophylaxis, hydration, pressure area care) is essential.
explanation.pearls: In suspected catatonia give IV lorazepam 1 to 2 mg as a challenge and observe over 10 minutes; avoid antipsychotics acutely because they can worsen or precipitate malignant catatonia.

subtopic_detail: Schizoaffective vs bipolar with psychotic features differentiation
stem:
A 26-year-old woman is referred to your community mental health clinic. Over the past 3 years she has had two clearly delineated episodes of elevated mood (each with reduced sleep, grandiose delusions, pressured speech, spending sprees and racing thoughts) lasting 3 weeks each, both fully resolving on quetiapine after 4 weeks of treatment. She has also had one 5 month period of persistent auditory hallucinations and paranoid delusions in the absence of any mood symptoms, occurring 6 months after her first mood episode.

Between all these episodes she has functioned well, held a stable job as a teaching assistant, and had no residual symptoms. She has no substance use disorder, no history of head injury, and no thyroid disease. She is not currently on any regular medication.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72/min, blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Euthymic, reality-oriented today; no active hallucinations or delusions; cognition intact on MoCA 28/30
data_table.Investigations: Routine bloods (FBC, U and E, LFTs, TSH, B12, folate) within normal limits; urine drug screen negative

lead_in: Which diagnosis best fits her presentation?

options.text: Bipolar I disorder with psychotic features as the sole diagnosis explaining all her episodes as the sole intervention
options.rationale: Bipolar I with psychotic features requires psychotic symptoms only during mood episodes; her 5 month euthymic psychotic period excludes this. (Source: DSM-5-TR Diagnostic and Statistical Manual)

options.text: Schizophrenia with superimposed episodes of mood disturbance as an isolated diagnosis as the sole intervention
options.rationale: Schizophrenia requires at least 6 months of symptoms with functional decline; her inter-episode functioning is preserved and mood episodes dominate. (Source: DSM-5-TR Diagnostic and Statistical Manual)

options.text: Brief psychotic disorder recurrent type with a separate independent bipolar I diagnosis running in parallel
options.rationale: Brief psychotic disorder lasts less than 1 month; 5 months of psychotic symptoms rules this out. (Source: DSM-5-TR Diagnostic and Statistical Manual)

options.text: Delusional disorder alongside a separate diagnosis of bipolar II disorder as best fit as the sole intervention
options.rationale: Delusional disorder does not feature prominent hallucinations or thought disorder; auditory hallucinations rule it out. (Source: DSM-5-TR Diagnostic and Statistical Manual)

options.text: Schizoaffective disorder bipolar type based on the 5 month psychotic period without mood symptoms plus discrete mood episodes with psychosis
options.rationale: DSM-5 schizoaffective disorder requires at least 2 weeks of psychotic symptoms without mood symptoms in the lifetime course alongside mood episodes overlapping with psychosis. (Source: DSM-5-TR Diagnostic and Statistical Manual)

explanation.summary: DSM-5-TR schizoaffective disorder requires: (A) an uninterrupted period of illness with a major mood episode concurrent with the psychosis criterion A of schizophrenia; (B) delusions or hallucinations for at least 2 weeks in the absence of a major mood episode during the lifetime; (C) mood episode symptoms are present for the majority of the total illness duration; (D) not explained by substances or medical condition. Schizoaffective bipolar type has manic or mixed episodes; depressive type has only major depressive episodes. Bipolar I disorder with psychotic features (in contrast) confines psychotic symptoms to mood episodes only. Schizophrenia requires 6 months of symptoms with prodrome or residual features and generally has poorer inter-episode functioning. Longitudinal course and periods of mood-independent psychosis separate these diagnoses.
key_points: Schizoaffective disorder needs 2+ weeks of psychosis without mood symptoms in the lifetime course.
Bipolar I with psychotic features confines psychosis to mood episodes.
Schizophrenia has 6 months of symptoms with functional decline.
Delusional disorder excludes prominent hallucinations or thought disorder.
explanation.pearls: A period of at least 2 weeks of psychosis with no concurrent mood symptoms in the setting of clear mood episodes points to schizoaffective disorder rather than bipolar with psychotic features.

subtopic_detail: Adult ADHD stimulant selection with driving occupation
stem:
A 34-year-old man is referred to your adult psychiatry service after formal assessment confirmed adult ADHD combined presentation. He has struggled with organisation, concentration and impulsivity since childhood and was untreated as a child. He works as a long-distance truck driver in New South Wales and often drives 10 hour shifts. His WURS and DIVA-5 scores support long-standing ADHD, and secondary causes have been excluded.

He has no history of psychosis, no substance use disorder, and no cardiovascular disease. Blood pressure is normal, ECG on referral is unremarkable, BMI 26 kg/m2. He is understandably concerned about maintaining his heavy-vehicle licence and asks about medication choice.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 68/min, blood pressure 122/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert, cooperative; no tremor; cardiovascular examination unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: ECG unremarkable; TFTs, B12, folate within normal limits; DIVA-5 supports ADHD combined presentation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy plan?

options.text: Long-acting methylphenidate (Concerta) started at low dose with formal notification to Roads and Maritime for a fitness-to-drive review before returning to driving
options.rationale: Long-acting methylphenidate is first-line for adult ADHD in Australia; driving with untreated or newly medicated ADHD requires notification of the licensing authority for heavy-vehicle categories under Austroads. (Source: RANZCP Adult ADHD Guideline; Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive)

options.text: Dexamfetamine 5 mg twice daily commenced with a plan to continue driving during titration with routine outpatient follow-up
options.rationale: Continuing heavy-vehicle driving during stimulant titration is not appropriate without a fitness-to-drive review; Austroads criteria are stricter for commercial licensing. (Source: Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive)

options.text: Atomoxetine 40 mg daily as first-line without cardiovascular considerations or driving review with routine outpatient follow-up
options.rationale: Atomoxetine is second-line for adult ADHD in Australia; stimulants are preferred first-line and driving still requires review. (Source: RANZCP Adult ADHD Guideline)

options.text: Bupropion sustained-release started as an off-label alternative to stimulants for immediate effect as the sole intervention
options.rationale: Bupropion is not approved and not preferred for adult ADHD in Australian guidance; stimulants are first-line. (Source: RANZCP Adult ADHD Guideline)

options.text: Modafinil 100 mg daily for narcolepsy-style wakefulness support without further titration with routine outpatient follow-up
options.rationale: Modafinil is not approved for ADHD in Australia; stimulants are first-line. (Source: RANZCP Adult ADHD Guideline)

explanation.summary: The RANZCP adult ADHD guideline recommends stimulants (long-acting methylphenidate or lisdexamfetamine) as first-line pharmacotherapy for adult ADHD, with atomoxetine or guanfacine as non-stimulant alternatives when stimulants are contraindicated or not tolerated. Baseline evaluation includes cardiovascular history, blood pressure, pulse, and ECG in those over 40 or with cardiac risk factors. Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive treats untreated symptomatic ADHD as a potential conditional licence issue, particularly for commercial vehicles; commercial drivers must have adequate symptom control and typically require fitness-to-drive certification from the treating clinician. Titration should occur off-driving where safety is a concern until effect and side-effects are stable.
key_points: Long-acting stimulants (methylphenidate, lisdexamfetamine) are first-line for adult ADHD.
Atomoxetine and guanfacine are non-stimulant alternatives.
Austroads fitness-to-drive review is required for commercial licence holders.
Baseline ECG for those over 40 or with cardiac risk factors.
explanation.pearls: For a truck driver with adult ADHD start long-acting methylphenidate at low dose and arrange formal Austroads fitness-to-drive review before returning to commercial driving.

stem:
A 58-year-old woman has severe recurrent major depressive disorder with three prior admissions, each requiring index ECT after failed pharmacological trials. Her most recent acute course of ECT 4 months ago produced remission after 9 treatments. She was discharged on venlafaxine 225 mg daily plus lithium 750 mg nocte. She has now presented to your outpatient clinic with re-emergent depressive symptoms (Hamilton-D 22) 3 months after the last acute ECT session and is beginning to describe passive suicidal ideation again.

She has full capacity today, is engaged in treatment planning, and has no active psychotic features. Her thyroid, B12 and folate are within normal limits. Adherence to medication has been checked and confirmed by her partner. She has no medical contraindications to further ECT.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 74/min, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Depressed affect; psychomotor slowing; no psychotic features; MoCA 27/30
data_table.Investigations: TFTs, B12, folate within normal limits; venlafaxine and lithium levels therapeutic

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Refer for vagal nerve stimulator implantation without further trial of ECT or medication changes
options.rationale: VNS is a later-line intervention and would not be considered before optimising ECT and pharmacotherapy. (Source: RANZCP Position Statement ECT)

options.text: Commence a course of maintenance ECT (typically weekly then tapered) alongside her current pharmacotherapy
options.rationale: Maintenance ECT is indicated for patients with repeated severe relapses after successful index ECT and inadequate response to pharmacotherapy alone; it reduces relapse rates in this group. (Source: RANZCP Position Statement ECT)

options.text: Increase venlafaxine to 300 mg daily and add mirtazapine 30 mg nocte with no ECT plan
options.rationale: Pharmacological augmentation has been optimised (venlafaxine plus lithium) and has failed to prevent relapse in a patient with three prior index ECT courses; maintenance ECT is the evidence-based next step. (Source: RANZCP Position Statement ECT)

options.text: Switch to a monoamine oxidase inhibitor after a suitable washout without proceeding to any form of ECT
options.rationale: MAOI switch is one option but requires washout risking further deterioration and has not been shown superior to maintenance ECT in this pattern. (Source: RANZCP Position Statement ECT)

options.text: Add cognitive behavioural therapy weekly without any change to biological treatment for 12 weeks
options.rationale: CBT is a useful adjunct but does not address the biological relapse pattern in severe recurrent depression with prior ECT-responsiveness. (Source: RANZCP Position Statement ECT)

explanation.summary: Maintenance ECT is offered to patients with severe recurrent depression, particularly those who have relapsed despite optimised pharmacotherapy after successful index ECT. Schedules typically start weekly for several weeks, then fortnightly, then monthly, individualised to relapse pattern. It requires informed consent at each session, ongoing capacity assessment, and continued treatment of medical comorbidities including cognitive monitoring. Common side effects include short-term memory impairment which is usually reversible. It is often used alongside optimised antidepressant and lithium therapy rather than as replacement.
key_points: Maintenance ECT is indicated for repeated relapse after successful index ECT.
Schedules typically taper from weekly to monthly.
Continued antidepressant and mood stabiliser therapy runs alongside.
Cognitive and cardiovascular monitoring is required.
explanation.pearls: For a patient relapsing 3 months after successful index ECT despite optimised venlafaxine plus lithium, maintenance ECT weekly with taper is the evidence-based intervention alongside continued pharmacotherapy.

subtopic_detail: TCA overdose management with subtle ECG changes
stem:
You are the emergency registrar at 2 am. A 22-year-old woman is brought in by ambulance 90 minutes after ingesting approximately 40 tablets of her grandmother's amitriptyline 25 mg (approximately 1 gram total). She is drowsy but rousable (GCS 13), warm and dry, and reports one episode of vomiting. She weighs 65 kg. Paracetamol level from arrival is negligible and her BSL is 5.8 mmol/L.

Her ECG shows sinus tachycardia at 122/min, QRS duration 108 ms (widening from a baseline 90 ms recorded 30 minutes ago), and QT interval 460 ms. There are no ventricular ectopics yet. Two large-bore cannulae are in place. She has not been given activated charcoal. Blood pressure is 108/64 mmHg. Anaesthetics and ICU have been paged.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 122/min, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: GCS 13; dilated pupils reactive to light; warm dry skin; no meningism; abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: Paracetamol negligible; BSL 5.8; ECG QRS 108 ms (up from 90); K 3.9 mmol/L (3.5-5.2); pH 7.34, HCO3 21 mmol/L (22-32)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Oral activated charcoal 50 g given to a drowsy patient without airway protection right now
options.rationale: Charcoal in a GCS 13 patient without protected airway risks aspiration; it may be considered after intubation within 1-2 hours of ingestion by expert decision. (Source: Australian Poisons Information Centre)

options.text: Physostigmine 1 mg IV to reverse the anticholinergic features seen in this presentation
options.rationale: Physostigmine is contraindicated in TCA overdose because of the risk of precipitating cardiac arrest, bradyarrhythmias and seizures. (Source: Australian Poisons Information Centre)

options.text: IV sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol (1-2 mmol/kg) bolus and prepare for airway management as GCS deteriorates
options.rationale: Progressive QRS widening in TCA overdose is a class-effect marker of sodium channel blockade and cardiotoxicity; IV sodium bicarbonate is the specific antidote and airway support anticipates seizure and coma. (Source: RCH CPG Amitriptyline/Tricyclic overdose; Australian Poisons Information Centre)

options.text: IV flumazenil 200 microgram bolus to reverse the reduced GCS quickly as the sole intervention
options.rationale: Flumazenil is not indicated for TCA toxicity; it can precipitate seizures and TCA already lowers seizure threshold. (Source: Australian Poisons Information Centre)

options.text: IV amiodarone 300 mg over 20 minutes to treat the sinus tachycardia and prevent ventricular arrhythmia
options.rationale: Class III antiarrhythmics can worsen TCA cardiotoxicity by prolonging QT further; specific therapy is bicarbonate not antiarrhythmic. (Source: Australian Poisons Information Centre)

explanation.summary: Amitriptyline and other TCAs cause toxicity through sodium channel blockade (myocardial), anticholinergic effects, alpha-1 blockade (hypotension) and CNS depression with seizure lowering. QRS above 100 ms predicts seizures and QRS above 160 ms predicts ventricular arrhythmias. The specific antidote is IV sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg boluses, aiming for narrowing of QRS, and arterial pH 7.5 to 7.55. Airway management is proactive because seizures and coma are common. Charcoal may be considered within 1 to 2 hours only in intubated patients.
key_points: QRS above 100 ms predicts seizures; above 160 ms predicts arrhythmia.
Specific antidote is IV sodium bicarbonate targeting QRS narrowing and pH 7.5-7.55.
Class I and III antiarrhythmics and physostigmine are contraindicated.
Charcoal only after airway protection within 1-2 hours.
explanation.pearls: In amitriptyline overdose a QRS widening to above 100 ms is the marker to give IV sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mmol/kg while preparing airway support; avoid flumazenil, physostigmine and class III antiarrhythmics.

stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 24-year-old man 6 months after commencing olanzapine 10 mg nightly for a first episode of schizophrenia. He is stable on the current dose with resolved positive symptoms and returning to work part time. He has gained 8 kg since starting olanzapine and his current BMI is 27 kg/m2. He has no personal history of type 2 diabetes but his father was diagnosed at age 45. He smokes 10 cigarettes daily and eats a takeaway-heavy diet.

He has had a full baseline metabolic screen before starting olanzapine including weight, waist circumference, blood pressure, fasting lipids, fasting glucose and prolactin. He now attends for routine follow up. He would like to continue olanzapine as it has clearly helped his symptoms and asks what monitoring he should have.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, blood pressure 132/84 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Weight 92 kg, waist circumference 98 cm, no extrapyramidal signs
data_table.Investigations: Baseline (6 months ago): fasting glucose 4.8 mmol/L, HbA1c 5.4 percent, total cholesterol 4.8 mmol/L, triglycerides 1.4 mmol/L, prolactin 320 mIU/L (<430)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate metabolic monitoring plan for this patient?

options.text: Fasting lipids, fasting glucose and HbA1c annually; weight and blood pressure at each mental state review
options.rationale: Metabolic bloods including lipids and glucose are required at 3 and 12 months in the first year, then annually; annually alone underuses early detection. (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Metabolic Monitoring Guidance)

options.text: Fasting lipids, glucose and HbA1c now and again at 12 months, then annually; weight and BP each visit
options.rationale: RANZCP schedule includes 3-month and 12-month metabolic bloods in year one then annually; 6-month timing captures the fast weight gain window for olanzapine. (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Metabolic Monitoring Guidance)

options.text: Cease olanzapine now and switch to aripiprazole because weight gain of over 5 kg mandates change
options.rationale: Switching is considered after ongoing metabolic derangement despite lifestyle intervention; a single 8 kg gain does not itself mandate a switch, especially in a well-responder. (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Metabolic Monitoring Guidance)

options.text: Repeat only prolactin and ECG now, deferring metabolic bloods until 12 months post-initiation
options.rationale: Prolactin is not the main monitor for olanzapine (a low-prolactin agent); metabolic bloods are the priority in the first year. (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Metabolic Monitoring Guidance)

options.text: Refer to endocrinology for glucose tolerance test now regardless of the current fasting glucose result today
options.rationale: OGTT is not routine; fasting glucose and HbA1c are the RANZCP monitoring standards. (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Metabolic Monitoring Guidance)

explanation.summary: Second-generation antipsychotics cause weight gain, insulin resistance and dyslipidaemia, most marked with olanzapine and clozapine. Baseline metabolic screen before starting includes weight, waist, blood pressure, fasting lipids, fasting glucose and HbA1c (plus prolactin if symptomatic). The recommended schedule is repeat at 3 months, at 6 months for high-risk agents, at 12 months, and annually thereafter, with weight and blood pressure at every visit. Persistent metabolic derangement despite lifestyle intervention triggers consideration of switching agent, adding metformin, or optimising cardiovascular risk factors.
key_points: Baseline metabolic screen before starting an antipsychotic.
Recheck at 3 months, 12 months in year 1, then annually.
High-risk agents (olanzapine, clozapine) warrant additional 6-month check.
Weight and BP at every visit; lifestyle counselling from initiation.
explanation.pearls: RANZCP metabolic monitoring for antipsychotics: fasting lipids, glucose, HbA1c at baseline, 3 months, 12 months and annually; add 6-month check for high-risk agents like olanzapine and clozapine.

stem:
A 42-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has been on lithium carbonate 750 mg nightly for 5 years with excellent mood stability. She has had no manic or depressive relapses in that time. Her last set of monitoring bloods 12 months ago showed lithium level 0.7 mmol/L (0.6-0.8), TSH 2.4 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), creatinine 78 micromol/L (45-90) and calcium 2.32 mmol/L (2.15-2.60). She attends your outpatient clinic for routine review; she has no symptoms of toxicity, no polyuria and no cognitive concerns.

She takes no other medications, does not smoke and drinks no alcohol. She is on a stable diet with regular fluid intake. There is no personal or family history of thyroid disease. She would like to know what long-term monitoring is required from here on.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72/min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: No tremor, no cognitive impairment, no goitre, no oedema
data_table.Investigations: 12 months ago: lithium 0.7 mmol/L; TSH 2.4 mIU/L; creatinine 78 micromol/L; calcium 2.32 mmol/L; today's clinical review only

lead_in: What is the most appropriate ongoing monitoring plan?

options.text: Check lithium level annually; renal, thyroid and parathyroid function only if symptoms of derangement develop
options.rationale: Renal, thyroid and calcium monitoring is required at least 6-monthly on long-term lithium regardless of symptoms; symptom-based only under-monitors known adverse effects. (Source: RANZCP Lithium Long Term Monitoring)

options.text: Repeat lithium level, urea and electrolytes, calcium and thyroid function tests every 3 months for the next year
options.rationale: 3-monthly is more frequent than required for stable long-term lithium; 6-monthly is the standard ongoing schedule. (Source: RANZCP Lithium Long Term Monitoring)

options.text: Repeat lithium level, urea and electrolytes, calcium and thyroid function every 6 months as long as she remains stable
options.rationale: The RANZCP schedule for stable long-term lithium is lithium level plus renal, thyroid and calcium every 6 months once beyond the first year. (Source: RANZCP Lithium Long Term Monitoring)

options.text: Cease lithium and switch to sodium valproate to avoid further renal exposure risk in the coming years
options.rationale: Switching a well-responder to another agent risks relapse; monitoring is preferred as long as renal function remains stable. (Source: RANZCP Lithium Long Term Monitoring)

options.text: Add annual glomerular filtration rate estimate but omit thyroid function tests because she is asymptomatic
options.rationale: Thyroid function is checked at least every 6 months on lithium because hypothyroidism is often subclinical initially. (Source: RANZCP Lithium Long Term Monitoring)

explanation.summary: Lithium requires ongoing monitoring because of its narrow therapeutic index (0.4-1.0 mmol/L for maintenance) and known long-term risks: reduced glomerular filtration, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, hypothyroidism, hyperparathyroidism and hypercalcaemia. Schedule after initial titration and 12 months of stability is lithium level plus urea, creatinine, calcium and TSH every 6 months. Any change in dose, addition of interacting medications (thiazides, ACE inhibitors, NSAIDs) or intercurrent illness (dehydration, vomiting, diarrhoea) prompts an interim level. Signs of toxicity include tremor, ataxia, confusion, seizures. Ensure adequate hydration and consistent salt intake.
key_points: 6-monthly lithium level plus renal, thyroid and calcium after year 1.
Interim level if dose change, intercurrent illness or new interacting drug.
Long-term risks include CKD, DI, hypothyroidism, hyperparathyroidism.
Therapeutic range for maintenance is 0.4-1.0 mmol/L.
explanation.pearls: Long-term lithium monitoring: lithium level plus urea, creatinine, calcium and TSH every 6 months once stable, with an interim level for any intercurrent illness or new interacting drug.

stem:
A 24-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder is stable on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily for the last 3 years after two hospitalisations for mania in her early 20s. She and her new partner have started discussing having a baby in the next 12 months. She currently uses no contraception and denies missed periods. Prior trials of lithium caused unacceptable tremor and cognitive slowing, and olanzapine caused significant weight gain. She has never been trialled on lamotrigine.

On examination she is euthymic with good insight. She has no active suicidal ideation. She is well engaged with her community mental health team. Her most recent valproate level was 550 micromol/L (300-700), FBC, LFTs and pregnancy test today are normal. She reads widely and asks specifically about the risks of continuing valproate through pregnancy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 74/min, blood pressure 116/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Euthymic, good insight, no suicidal or homicidal ideation
data_table.Investigations: Valproate 550 micromol/L (300-700); full blood count within normal limits; liver function tests within normal limits; beta hCG negative today

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Continue valproate at current dose through pregnancy because the mood benefits outweigh teratogenic risk for a stable patient
options.rationale: Valproate has a 10 percent rate of major congenital malformations and up to 40 percent rate of neurodevelopmental effects; continuation through planned pregnancy is not consistent with TGA and RANZCP guidance. (Source: TGA Valproate and Pregnancy)

options.text: Halve valproate dose to 500 mg daily immediately to reduce dose-dependent teratogenicity and continue conception planning
options.rationale: Lower valproate doses reduce but do not eliminate teratogenic risk; dose reduction alone is inadequate. (Source: TGA Valproate and Pregnancy)

options.text: Add 5 mg folate daily and continue valproate through the first trimester to reduce neural tube defect risk
options.rationale: High-dose folate is recommended alongside valproate but does not offset the teratogenic risk profile of the drug itself; valproate substitution is the priority. (Source: TGA Valproate and Pregnancy)

options.text: Ensure reliable contraception, plan cross-titration to lamotrigine before conception, and start 5 mg folate daily
options.rationale: Valproate in a woman of childbearing potential requires effective contraception and consideration of a safer alternative such as lamotrigine before conception; folate 5 mg daily is added periconception. (Source: TGA Valproate and Pregnancy)

options.text: Cease valproate abruptly today and monitor mood over the next 4 to 6 weeks without any bridging medication or plan
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation risks manic relapse; cross-titration to lamotrigine (or alternative) is safer than washout. (Source: TGA Valproate and Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Sodium valproate is highly teratogenic: around 10 percent risk of major congenital malformations (neural tube defects, cardiac, craniofacial, limb) and up to 40 percent risk of neurodevelopmental effects including autism spectrum disorder. TGA and RANZCP guidance requires reliable contraception for all women of childbearing potential on valproate; a pregnancy prevention program with documented shared decision-making should be in place. When pregnancy is planned or possible, cross-titrate to a safer alternative (lamotrigine for bipolar maintenance, lithium as second-line, olanzapine short-term). Folate 5 mg daily is recommended if valproate cannot be stopped (higher than the standard 0.5 mg periconception dose). Any discovered pregnancy on valproate warrants urgent specialist review.
key_points: Valproate has 10 percent major malformation risk and up to 40 percent neurodevelopmental risk.
Reliable contraception required for all women of childbearing potential.
Cross-titrate to lamotrigine before planned conception where possible.
5 mg daily folate if valproate cannot be stopped.
explanation.pearls: Sodium valproate has around 10 percent major malformation and up to 40 percent neurodevelopmental risk; substitute to lamotrigine before planned conception and use 5 mg daily folate periconception.
